title: Pretrained models for text and speech
summary: Encoder-only (BERT), decoder-only (GPT) and encoder-decoder models, language modelling, using and fine-tuning models with Hugging Face, sound as data (waveforms, sampling, spectrograms), and speech models HuBERT, Whisper and audio-LLMs.
syllabus: IOAI 4A5 Pre-trained Language Models (open-source and API-based)
IOAI 4B2 Audio Models: Qwen-Audio, Whisper, Voxtral

lessons.title: BERT, GPT and language modelling
lessons.summary: Encoder-only models pretrained by filling in masked words, decoder-only models that predict the next token, and how their attention masks differ.
objectives: You can describe masked language modelling and the 80/10/10 rule
You can explain how the [CLS] vector is used for classification
You can write a sentence probability as a product of next-token probabilities and explain perplexity
You can match encoder-only and decoder-only models to tasks

concepts.name: Masked language modelling
concepts.explain: BERT is pretrained by hiding some tokens and predicting them from both left and right context. 15% of tokens are selected; of these, 80% become [MASK], 10% a random token and 10% stay unchanged, so the model cannot rely on seeing [MASK] at fine-tuning time. Because it sees both sides, BERT builds rich representations but cannot generate text left to right.
concepts.analogy: A cloze passage in an English paper: fill in the blanks using the words before and after.

visual.shows: A sentence with some tokens masked and illustrative top-5 predictions with probabilities for each mask; a sampler panel shows the 80/10/10 outcome for selected tokens.
visual.interaction: Click words to mask them; resample the 80/10/10 choices; compare predictions with left-only context.
visual.aha: Seeing both sides of a gap gives far better guesses than seeing only the left.

concepts.name: [CLS] and fine-tuning
concepts.explain: BERT adds a [CLS] token at the start; after the encoder, its final vector serves as a summary of the whole input. For classification, a small linear head on the [CLS] vector is trained along with (usually) the whole encoder at a small learning rate.
concepts.analogy: The class monitor who listens to everyone and then reports the class's overall view to the teacher.

visual.shows: Tokens flowing through stacked encoder blocks with the [CLS] position highlighted at each layer, then into a linear head and softmax.
visual.interaction: Hover layers to see that [CLS] attends to all tokens; toggle 'freeze encoder' to see trainable parameter counts change.
visual.aha: One special token's output becomes the sentence embedding for downstream tasks.

concepts.name: Next-token probabilities
concepts.explain: A language model assigns a probability to every possible next token given the text so far. A sentence's probability is the product of these conditional probabilities (the chain rule). Training maximises the probability of real text, which is self-supervised learning on huge corpora. Generating text one token at a time, each conditioned on all the tokens before it, is called autoregressive generation, so GPT is an autoregressive decoder while BERT is a bidirectional encoder.
concepts.analogy: Predictive text on your phone, scaled up to everything ever written online.

visual.shows: A prompt box and bars of next-token probabilities from a small bigram/trigram model trained on a toy Singapore-themed corpus, with a running sentence probability as tokens are appended.
visual.interaction: Type or click tokens to extend the prompt; switch between bigram and trigram contexts.
visual.aha: Generating text is repeatedly picking from a next-token distribution.

concepts.name: Encoder versus decoder attention
concepts.explain: GPT-style decoder-only models use a causal mask so each token sees only earlier tokens, which allows left-to-right generation. BERT-style encoders see the full sequence in both directions, which is better for understanding tasks but cannot generate. Perplexity, the exponential of the average negative log-probability, measures how 'surprised' a language model is.
concepts.analogy: Writing a story one sentence at a time without peeking ahead (GPT) versus editing a finished story where you can see everything (BERT).

visual.shows: Side-by-side attention-mask grids for encoder (full) and decoder (lower-triangular), with which tokens contribute to a selected position, and a perplexity readout for sample sentences.
visual.interaction: Click a position to highlight what it can see; compare perplexity of a fluent and a scrambled sentence.
visual.aha: The mask, not the block design, is the main difference between BERT and GPT.

checkpoint_focus: BERT is bidirectional; GPT is causal
Chain rule of probability for sequences

lessons.title: Encoder-decoder models
lessons.summary: Sequence-to-sequence Transformers for translation, summarisation, captioning and speech recognition, with cross-attention linking the two halves.
objectives: You can describe the encoder-decoder architecture and cross-attention
You can match tasks to encoder-only, decoder-only or encoder-decoder models
You can name examples (T5, BART, MarianMT, Whisper)

concepts.name: Cross-attention aligns output with input
concepts.explain: In an encoder-decoder model, the encoder reads the whole input; the decoder generates the output token by token, and its cross-attention layers use the decoder's states as queries and the encoder's outputs as keys and values. Each output word can therefore look at the most relevant input words.
concepts.analogy: An interpreter listening to the whole speech, then glancing back at their notes for the relevant part as they translate each sentence.

visual.shows: A source sentence (English) and target sentence (Malay or Chinese) with an illustrative cross-attention heat map; clicking a target word highlights the source words it attends to.
visual.interaction: Click target words; switch examples with word-order differences.
visual.aha: Cross-attention learns a soft alignment between input and output.

concepts.name: Three families of Transformers
concepts.explain: Transformers come in three families that match three task shapes. Encoder-only models (BERT) suit understanding tasks such as classification and tagging, and decoder-only models (GPT, Llama, Qwen) suit generation and underlie most LLMs. Encoder-decoder models (T5, BART, Whisper) suit turning one sequence into another, such as translation, summarisation, captioning and speech-to-text.
concepts.analogy: A reader, a writer and a translator.

visual.shows: Three columns with block diagrams and example models, and task cards to drop into the right column.
visual.interaction: Drag task cards (sentiment, chatbot, translation, NER, speech-to-text, summarisation) into a family; feedback explains the choice.
visual.aha: Architecture follows the task's input-output shape.

checkpoint_focus: Encoder reads full input, decoder generates
Cross-attention: queries from decoder, keys/values from encoder
Vision-language and speech use the same pattern

lessons.title: Using and fine-tuning models with Hugging Face
lessons.summary: Pipelines, tokenizers and AutoModels, what the tokenizer outputs, fine-tuning with labels and -100, and calling API-based models.
objectives: You can run a Hugging Face pipeline for a task
You can explain input_ids, attention_mask and labels
You can outline a fine-tuning loop (or Trainer) for sequence classification
You can explain ignore_index = -100 for padded label positions

concepts.name: From text to prediction in Hugging Face
concepts.explain: A pipeline bundles a tokenizer, a model and post-processing: pipeline('sentiment-analysis')(text) returns a label and score. Underneath, the tokenizer produces input_ids and an attention_mask, the model outputs logits, and post-processing applies softmax and maps ids to labels.
concepts.analogy: A drinks vending machine: you press one button, but inside there is a cup dispenser, a mixer and a pump.

visual.shows: A sentence passing through tokenizer (showing input_ids and attention_mask), model (logits), softmax (probabilities) and label mapping, with the code line for each stage.
visual.interaction: Step through stages; edit the text; switch the task (classification, NER, summarisation) to see different post-processing.
visual.aha: Every pipeline is tokenise → model → post-process, and you can call each stage yourself.

concepts.name: Fine-tuning and ignored labels
concepts.explain: To fine-tune, load a pretrained model with a new head (e.g. AutoModelForSequenceClassification with num_labels), tokenize your data, and train with a small learning rate, either with your own loop or the Trainer. For token-level tasks and language modelling, label positions set to -100 (padding or special tokens) are skipped by the cross-entropy loss.
concepts.analogy: Marking only the questions a student actually attempted, skipping blank answer spaces.

visual.shows: A token sequence with its labels row; -100 positions are greyed and excluded from the per-token loss bars and the averaged loss.
visual.interaction: Toggle padding and special tokens; change which positions are -100 and see the loss change.
visual.aha: -100 is PyTorch's default ignore_index, so padding never contributes to the loss.

lessons.title: Sound as data: waveforms and spectrograms
lessons.summary: Sampling rate and the Nyquist limit, waveforms, the short-time Fourier transform, spectrograms and the mel scale.
objectives: You can explain sampling rate and the Nyquist limit
You can describe how a spectrogram is built from short windows
You can explain why mel spectrograms are used for speech
You can compute audio tensor sizes

concepts.name: Sampling a waveform
concepts.explain: Sound is air pressure changing over time; a microphone records it as numbers sampled many times per second (16,000 per second is common for speech, so 10 seconds is 160,000 numbers). To capture a frequency, you must sample at more than twice that frequency (the Nyquist limit), otherwise it appears as a false lower frequency (aliasing).
concepts.analogy: A video of a spinning wheel at too low a frame rate makes the wheel look like it is turning backwards.

visual.shows: A continuous sine wave, the sample points taken at the chosen rate, and the wave reconstructed from those samples, which shows aliasing when the rate is too low.
visual.interaction: Slide the signal frequency and the sampling rate; mix two frequencies.
visual.aha: The sampling rate caps the highest frequency you can capture.

concepts.name: Building a spectrogram
concepts.explain: A spectrogram slices audio into short overlapping windows (e.g. 25 ms, hopping by 10 ms), computes the strength of each frequency in each window with a Fourier transform, and stacks the results into an image: time across, frequency up, loudness as colour. The mel scale spaces frequency bins the way human hearing does, giving more detail at low frequencies. Many speech models take log-mel spectrograms as input.
concepts.analogy: Sheet music for any sound: time runs left to right and pitch goes up and down.

visual.shows: A synthetic waveform (a chirp plus a tone), a window sliding along it, the frequency bars for the current window, and the spectrogram image filling column by column; a toggle warps the frequency axis to mel.
visual.interaction: Play the sweep; change window size and hop length; toggle mel scaling and log amplitude.
visual.aha: A spectrogram turns sound into an image, so vision-style models can process audio.

checkpoint_focus: Nyquist: sample at more than twice the highest frequency

lessons.title: Speech models: HuBERT, Whisper and audio LLMs
lessons.summary: Self-supervised audio encoders like HuBERT, encoder-decoder speech recognition with Whisper, and audio-language models such as Qwen-Audio and Voxtral.
objectives: You can explain HuBERT's masked prediction of hidden units
You can describe Whisper's encoder-decoder pipeline from log-mel input to text tokens
You can describe how audio LLMs connect an audio encoder to a language model
You can choose a model for transcription, audio classification or audio question answering

concepts.name: HuBERT: BERT for audio
concepts.explain: HuBERT splits audio into short frames, assigns each frame a discrete 'hidden unit' label by clustering (k-means), then masks spans of frames and trains a Transformer to predict the units of the masked frames, just like BERT's masked words. The resulting encoder produces audio embeddings useful for speech recognition, speaker or emotion classification.
concepts.analogy: Learning a language's sounds by listening to hours of radio and guessing muffled syllables from context, without any transcripts.

visual.shows: A waveform split into frames, frame colours showing cluster ids, a masked span, and the model's predicted unit distribution for masked frames.
visual.interaction: Step through clustering, masking and prediction; change the mask span length.
visual.aha: The same masked-prediction trick works for any data you can cut into tokens, including sound.

concepts.name: Whisper's pipeline
concepts.explain: Whisper converts 30-second audio chunks into log-mel spectrograms, encodes them with a Transformer encoder, and a decoder generates text tokens with cross-attention to the audio. Special task tokens tell the decoder which language and whether to transcribe or translate to English.
concepts.analogy: A court stenographer who listens to a recording and types it out, told beforehand whether to transcribe it as is or translate it.

visual.shows: Audio → log-mel image → encoder blocks → decoder generating tokens one by one, with the special task tokens at the start of the output sequence.
visual.interaction: Step through; toggle transcribe/translate and the language token to see how the output changes.
visual.aha: Speech recognition is just an encoder-decoder Transformer with a spectrogram as the 'source sentence'.

concepts.name: Audio language models
concepts.explain: Audio LLMs such as Qwen-Audio and Voxtral pair an audio encoder (often Whisper-style) with a large language model. The audio embeddings are projected into the LLM's token space and placed alongside text tokens, so the LLM can answer questions about the sound, summarise a meeting or follow spoken instructions.
concepts.analogy: Giving a very knowledgeable writer a pair of ears, plus an interpreter who turns sounds into words the writer understands.

visual.shows: Audio → encoder → projector → a sequence mixing audio tokens and text-prompt tokens → LLM decoder → answer, with tensor shapes.
visual.interaction: Click each component to see what it does and whether it is frozen or fine-tuned in typical training.
visual.aha: Multimodal LLMs reuse a pretrained encoder and a pretrained LLM, joined by a small learned adapter.

checkpoint_focus: HuBERT = BERT-style masking on audio frames
Whisper: log-mel → encoder → decoder with task tokens
Using Hugging Face pipelines for ASR and audio classification
